sittings.bodyEn: Attentional space grows and shrinks with mental energy. Enough sleep can expand it by more than half, and real breaks can do related work. When the space is larger by about sixty percent, output on a demanding task can rise by about as much. Hyperfocus spends the pool, because holding yourself to one task against distractions is tiring, and the space contracts as the pool drops. Scatterfocus and true rest put energy back. A short inward break is part of focusing, because the next block needs the energy the last one spent.

terms.hook: The pool that sets how large attentional space is and how long focus can last.

sittings.bodyEn: Switching often, and being unable to stay with one thing, means the energy pool is low. Losing your intentions and working in a reactive way is the same signal. So is moving much slower than usual, such as rereading one important note several times. Choosing mindless work, or slipping into scatterfocus without deciding to, means you should recharge on purpose. Work you care about drains you more slowly, and the mind wanders less during a task you genuinely enjoy. The more you must push yourself, the sooner these signs arrive.

terms.hook: Fast switching, lost intentions, slow rereading, mindless tasks, or an unchosen wander.

sittings.bodyEn: A refreshing break is low-effort and habitual, something you actually want, and a chore only when you truly enjoy that chore. That mix is pleasurably effortless, so the mind can wander forward and still have fuel when you return. Mail, news, and feeds still spend attention, and they leave you on autopilot when the work resumes. Choose one activity you can do once or twice where you work: a walk, a workout, a short meditation, fun reading, music, a podcast, a person who energizes you, or a small creative hobby. Set the intention to do it tomorrow. During the pocket, leave the screen alone and let the break be the break.

terms.hook: A wanted, low-effort activity that spends no attention on a feed.

sittings.bodyEn: Take a break at least every ninety minutes, and take about fifteen minutes off for each hour you work. Across a usual day that looks like a real lunch plus a short morning break and a short afternoon break. Energy moves in roughly ninety-minute waves, including during sleep, so a dip of twenty or thirty minutes is a normal time to step back. Break when focus dips or when a big task ends, because a finished task leaves less residue in the wander. If you are an introvert in a loud social room, or the project fails to motivate you, shorten the interval, because heavier self-control drains the pool faster. The most productive slice of one tracking app's users averaged about seventeen minutes off after about fifty-two minutes on, which is a useful personal test. If you lead people, hire for genuine care about the work, because later advice cannot manufacture focus in a job someone is only enduring.

terms.hook: A natural energy cycle, with a break at least once each wave and about fifteen minutes off per hour.

sittings.bodyEn: The best moment to break is before you feel the need, just as thirst usually means you are already short on water. By the time fatigue is obvious, focus has already slipped. Low-energy stretches leave the mind less inhibited, so more ideas can surface. Use that dip for scatterfocus, and save the hard analytic push for a higher-energy hour. In the morning, watch the rise and fall and step back as the drop starts. Afternoons bounce less predictably, so keep a similar rhythm, and use the coffee, the lunch, or the walk you already take, with the phone left behind.

terms.hook: Step back before fatigue shows, and use the dip for a chosen wander.

sittings.bodyEn: A personal rule in the chapter, offered without a lab citation, says each missed hour of sleep costs about two hours of productivity the next day. A deficit can shrink attentional space by as much as sixty percent, and complex work can take more than twice as long. You also survey that space less often, and you rate your output as higher than it is. Mindless copying can survive the shrink, while a hard problem needs the space that sleep protects. Short sleep also brings more pressure, shorter focus, more time on social feeds, a worse mood, easier tasks, and more hours online. Dreaming lights the same regions as scatterfocus, only more strongly, so a full night both recharges you and keeps connecting dots.

terms.hook: Lost sleep that can shrink attentional space by more than half and stretch complex work.

sittings.bodyEn: By evening the pool is low, so the night runs on autopilot unless the sequence is set ahead of time. Build a short unwind that can include reading, a few minutes of meditation, disconnecting from screens, or a warm drink without caffeine. Take the television out of the bedroom, because it is a brighter object than sleep. Most people need about eight hours, and a midnight bedtime only works when the morning can move later. The wake time is often fixed, so the flexible piece is the evening routine that gets you into bed early enough for those eight hours. Keep the same sequence each night until it runs without a fresh decision.

terms.hook: A set unwind, with the bright screen out of the bedroom, that makes a full night likely.

sittings.bodyEn: Rest feels guilty when the list is longer than the day, because a break looks like lost output. The energy pool is limited, and when it is empty the focus is empty with it. A break is what keeps you from hitting that wall. Every rest trades a slice of time for energy, whether the rest is fifteen minutes or a night of sleep, and the energy is the return on that time. The busier the stretch, the more you need the step back, because overload is when a wider view still changes what you do next. Look back at a week when your energy was high, note the breaks or movement that were present, and repeat those conditions on purpose.

terms.hook: A break or a night of sleep that spends time and returns the fuel focus needs.

sittings.bodyEn: A break restores attention when it is easy, wanted, and free of a feed that still spends the pool. The working rhythm is a step back at least every ninety minutes, for about fifteen minutes per hour of work. The useful moment is before you feel empty, and the low dip is a good time to scatter attention. Sleep is the larger version of the same trade, and a deficit shrinks the space you are trying to use. A night routine is what makes that sleep likely when willpower is already gone. On the fullest days the guilt about resting is the cue to rest.
sittings.prompt: What makes a work break actually recharge attention?
choices: Checking news and messages so the inbox looks clear
A low-effort activity you want, with no feed spending attention
A second complex task that feels productive
Waiting until you are already too tired to continue
